newsitem.title: FRANCE: French right hammers on power-sharing, jobs.
newsitem.headline: French right hammers on power-sharing, jobs.

text.p: France's centre-right leaders hammered home a warning against power-sharing with the left on Wednesday, four days before the first round of a parliamentary election, and painted a rosy picture of economic recovery.
Sensing a tight race, ministers piled in behind conservative President Jacques Chirac's message to voters that France could only defend its interests in Europe if it spoke with a single voice.
Foreign Minister Herve de Charette said if the opposition Socialists and Communists won the May 25/June 1 election, "one can easily see a danger of France growing weaker".
"That would lead to difficult and complicated negotiations in fields where it is not easy to defend France's interests," he told Radio Monte Carlo.

Chirac delivered an upbeat assessment of the economy to the last cabinet meeting before polling day, stressing that the "spirit of enterprise and the spirit of conquest were back", government spokesman Alain Lamassoure told reporters.

Socialist opposition leader Lionel Jospin said the campaign against "cohabitation", the French term for power-sharing between a president and government of opposing parties, showed the right was running scared.
"It carries no weight (because) no one can put the French people under duress. In this election, the French people will express themselves freely," Jospin told a news conference.

The Socialists and Communists have said they would reject any further austerity measures to qualify France for a single European currency, and blamed the government for a postwar record 12.8 percent unemployment.
Justice Minister Jacques Toubon acknowledged concern in the ruling coalition at the prospect of a very close outcome.
"The election is tight," he told Europe 1 radio. "We would be most imprudent to be boastful or complacent."

He pointed to differences between the Socialists, who support the euro with conditions, and the Communists, who oppose it, and divergent positions on privatisation taken by different Socialist politicians.

French financial markets were stable on Wednesday, with the franc steady against the German mark and the Paris bourse up 1.1 percent buoyed by Wall Street's rally after the Federal Reserve Board decided against raising interest rates.

Chirac, speaking just before meeting German Chancellor Helmut Kohl at his Elysee presidential palace on Tuesday, said he would personally ensure France met its European commitments, a reference to fulfilling terms for the single currency.

Opinion polls released last weekend before a legal ban on publication of such surveys showed the centre-right in the lead but the combined forces of Socialists, Communists and ecologists gaining ground and within striking distance of a victory.
No more polls may be published before the June 1 conclusion of the two-round election, although surveys continue to be taken and some may be visible on the Internet.
De Charette said a leftist win would lead to "confusion within the government and conflict with the president.

"We have several important deadlines ahead of us, concerning European institutional reforms, NATO reforms and enlargement, and European economic and monetary union. Can you imagine having a head of state who thinks in one fashion and a prime minister who thinks in another?" he said.
On the economic front, Chirac trumpeted two big export contracts signed just in time for the election --- a major sale of Airbus planes to China and a warship deal with Saudi Arabia.
"France must look for growth wherever it can be found and these examples show we can be the best if there is a sufficient political driving force," Lamassoure quoted him as saying.
